newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr shows resilience despite risks.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr shows resilience despite risks.

text.p: The Australian dollar spent a holiday-hit Monday session consolidating an offshore rally, but lacked the momentum to extend the bounce to safe territory.

The currency's come-back from a US$0.7815 low repaired some of the technical damage done by last week's plunge from 79 and encouraged exporters to lift their bids for forex cover. There were also expectations of further samurai demand, although the dollar still lived largely at the whim of a volatile US$/yen.
A roomy 5.8 percent rise in domestic mortgage commitments for September, reported today, also leant the dollar support by providing another portent of a housing sector recovery.

By 4.30 pm (0530 GMT) the local dollar was resting at US$0.7875/80 having spent the entire day in a cramped 10-tick range. That was up on Friday's late US$0.7832/37 and not far distant from the US$0.7883/88 held this time last week.
It remained well adrift on the crosses, however, as the market fretted about Japan's apparent change of heart against a further weakening in the yen.

The dollar had steadied at 87.95/05 yen in late trade from 87.90/00 here Friday, but was a world away from last week's highs atop 90.00 yen. It also stablised in trade weighted terms, edging up to 58.0 from a previous 57.8 finish.

The currency's rally from Friday's lows came courtesy of exporter bids, which held the line at US$0.7815, and later European and U.S. bank buying, partly linked to a 20 billion yen dual currency samurai issue.
Dealers said another issue was thought to have gone through the market today suggesting Japanese demand was holding up well despite the recent narrowing in the dollar's yield advantage.

Domestic yields were on a major downtrend thanks to subdued inflation and last week's cut in official cash rates, In contrast, Japanese bond prices had leapt when authorities there turned more upbeat on the economy than the market was used to.

Despite the narrowing, domestic yields were still far above those in Japan and offered a healthy premium in real term to U.S. bonds since inflation here was expected to undercut that in the U.S. for the next year at least.

Dealers said bulls were hopeful the A$ premium would continue to attract Japanese fund flows which had picked up substantially in the last fortnight, as reflected in the issue of around 175 billion yen worth of dual currency samurai bonds.
Another cut in domestic rates might threaten the flow, but few analysts saw much chance of a move until February or March giving the dollar a few months grace.
Today's housing finance data, although typically of only secondary importance to markets, supported the case for expecting the next easing, if at all, in 1997.

The 5.8 percent rise in commitments was at the top end of forecasts and turned the trend firmly positive. The strength was tempered by the fact a sizeable 30 percent of the overall increase was again due to refinancing, which rose 6.4 percent.
However, commitments for the construction of dwellings did rise 2.4 percent and the purchase of new dwellings was up 11.7 percent. In annual terms, overall commitments were some 15.4 percent higher.
"There are encouraging signs of a sustained recovery in the housing market," said Steve Koukoulas, chief economist at Citibank Australia.
That would feed into bricks and mortar construction and into retail sales through purchases of new appliances etc.
And, since September, the economy had enjoyed further cuts in mortgage rates which should help keep the upturn alive.

"Housing investment is poised to contribute nearly half a percentage point to overall GDP in 1997 and, along with business investment, should be a main driver of a solid recovery," said Koukoulas. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
